summary: Defines a YANG data model for managing IP implementations, including configuration data and state data. It was replaced by RFC 8344.

plainLanguage.summary: A standard form lets tools read and change the IP settings on a device. It was later replaced by a newer form.

questions: how to configure ip with netconf
subtitle: A standard way to configure and monitor IP settings on network devices.

tldr.problem: Network operators need a standard way to configure and check the status of IP addresses, routing, and address resolution on routers and servers. Each device vendor had proprietary management methods.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7277 defines the ietf-ip YANG module, which augments the interface model to add configuration containers for IPv4 and IPv6, address lists, neighbor mappings, and state containers showing what is actually running.
tldr.outcome: Tools like NETCONF can now read and write IP configuration on any device that implements the model, improving interoperability. It was replaced by RFC 8344.

today: RFC 7277 is a Proposed Standard that defines the ietf-ip YANG module for IP management. It was replaced by RFC 8344.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 7277 defines the ietf-ip YANG module, a data model for managing IP implementations. YANG is a data modeling language that defines how to structure configuration and operational state data. This RFC specifies what parameters must be included when managing IP, how they are organized, and how they map to existing management standards like IP-MIB.

The model covers IPv4 and IPv6 configuration per interface (enabling the address family, setting forwarding, configuring addresses and MTU, and mapping IP addresses to link-layer addresses), and it provides corresponding state data showing what is actually running.
sections.plainLanguage: A data model is like a standard form that describes all the IP settings you might want to configure on a network device. This RFC says what that form should look like.

sections.title: The Data Model Structure
sections.content:
The ietf-ip YANG module augments (adds to) the interface model defined in RFC 7223. For each interface, it defines two container nodes, one for IPv4 and one for IPv6. Each container holds configuration data such as whether the address family is enabled, whether forwarding is on, the interface MTU in octets, a list of configured addresses (with prefix length or netmask), and a list of static neighbor mappings (IP address to link-layer address, like ARP entries).

The module also defines corresponding operational state containers, which are read-only and show the running configuration, actual addresses in use, which addresses came from DHCP or autoconfiguration, and the current neighbor cache.
sections.plainLanguage: The model has two parts: configuration (what you want), and state (what is actually running). For each address family, it tracks addresses, whether forwarding is on, and neighbor mappings.

sections.title: IPv4 and IPv6 Configuration
sections.content:
The IPv4 container holds a boolean enabled leaf (default true), a forwarding leaf, an MTU ranging from 68 to maximum octets, a list of addresses (each with an IPv4 address and subnet mask or prefix length), and neighbor entries for ARP resolution.

The IPv6 container is similar but has a larger MTU range (1280 to maximum), and adds duplicate address detection parameters and an autoconfiguration container. IPv6 addresses in configuration require only the address and prefix length. Autoconfiguration allows control over whether to create global addresses and temporary privacy addresses (RFC 4941), and sets their lifetimes.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv4 and IPv6 are configured nearly the same way: you turn them on, set an MTU, add addresses, and for IPv6 you can also turn on auto-address-creation.

sections.title: Operational State and Origins
sections.content: The state containers are read-only and show what is actually operationally used. For each address, a state node records its origin: static (manually configured), dhcp (from DHCP), link-layer (IPv6 address with an embedded MAC), or random (IPv6 privacy or link-local). Similarly, the neighbor state shows whether a mapping is static or dynamic (learned via ARP or Neighbor Discovery). IPv6 state includes the address status (preferred, deprecated, tentative) and neighbor state (reachable, stale, incomplete).
sections.plainLanguage: The state shows where each address came from (you set it, DHCP gave it, or it was auto-generated) and whether neighbors are currently reachable.

sections.title: Relationship to IP-MIB and NETCONF
sections.content: RFC 7277 maps each data node to equivalent objects in IP-MIB (RFC 4293), the SNMP management standard for IP. For example, the ipv4/address list maps to ipAddressEntry in the MIB, and neighbor lists map to ipNetToPhysicalTable. This mapping ensures that devices implementing the YANG model can also satisfy SNMP queries for the same data. The model is intended to be used with NETCONF (RFC 6241) for configuration management.
sections.plainLanguage: The same information can be retrieved via SNMP or NETCONF, so tools can use whichever protocol the device supports.

sections.title: Configuration Example
sections.content: The RFC includes an example NETCONF reply showing configuration and operational state for an ethernet interface eth0. Configuration shows the interface has IPv4 address 192.0.2.1/24 and IPv6 address 2001:db8::10/32. Operational state shows actual IPv4 forwarding is false, actual MTU is 1500, there is an ARP neighbor 192.0.2.2 with link-layer address 00:01:02:03:04:05, and there are two IPv6 addresses (one static, one from DHCP) with neighbors in various states.
sections.plainLanguage: Real example data shows how a router stores both what you told it to do (config) and what is actually happening (state).
